sources.headline: Paramount and Warner Bros merge into one Hollywood giant
sources.text:
Paramount on Tuesday finalized its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing a hostile acquisition that was months in the making and almost faltered at several hurdles.
The takeover cost a total of around $81 billion (roughly €72 billion), or almost $111 billion including the Warner Bros. debts passed on as part of the deal.
The merger brings together two of the oldest US filmmaking studios and will form a new giant called Skydance Corporation.
Why Skydance Corp.? Who's behind the new behemoth?
The new name Skydance hails from billionaire investor David Ellison, who first bought out Paramount and its subsidiaries and then moved on to target the much larger fish that is Warner Bros.
The bid faced stiff competition in a bidding war with Netflix, and later scrutiny from US regulators and politicians, but ultimately went through.
"Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," said Ellison, whose family has ties to US President Donald Trump.
Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker SKYD, while Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders will receive about $31 per share.
The deal closed less than a week after a federal judge in California approved a settlement between Paramount and 12 US states that had sued to block the transaction on antitrust grounds.
As well as the two giant film studios, Paramount Pictures and Warner Bros. Pictures, the deal also brings together the CBS News and CNN news networks, and the HBO and CBS television brands. Ellison says he plans to merge the subscription streaming platforms Paramount+ and HBO Max.
Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO of the new company. Former Mattel boss Ynon Kreiz is operating as co-CEO in charge of day-to-day operations.
Skydance Corp. looks set to have a total revenue in the region of $70 billion, based on the performance to date of its component parts. It says it's targeting cost savings of around $6 billion within three years as it takes advantage of overlaps created by the merger.
Edited by: Sean Sinico

sources.headline: Paramount completes takeover of Warner Bros, creating media behemoth Skydance
Paramount and Warner Bros complete merger to form Hollywood giant Skydance
sources.text:
Paramount closed its $81 billion (€72bn) purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, the companies announced on Tuesday, forming a new Hollywood giant called Skydance.
The merger brings HBO Max, films ranging from "Harry Potter" to "Sinners", and networks including CNN under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and titles such as "Top Gun" and "The Godfather".
“Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” CEO David Ellison said in a statement.
The deal further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. Ellison's Skydance bought Paramount in an $8bn (€7.1bn) deal last year, and set its sights on Warner soon afterwards.
What followed was a tumultuous, yearlong fight over Warner's fate. Including billions of dollars in debt, Paramount's buyout of Warner amounts to nearly $111bn (€98.6bn).
The combined company will have nearly $70bn (€62.5bn) in annual revenue and is targeting more than $6bn (€5.4bn) in annual cost savings within three years. Ellison will serve as chairman and CEO, while former Mattel chief Ynon Kreiz will oversee day-to-day operations and the integration of the two businesses.
Ellison also plans to merge Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single streaming service over time. Skydance shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Tuesday under the ticker “SKYD”.
A bidding war with Netflix
The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war.
Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management "never engaged meaningfully" with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company, including networks such as CNN and Discovery.
The companies spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer on the table, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually raised its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix opted to bow out of the race. Warner and Paramount signed a merger agreement in late February.
Hollywood stars speak out
From awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known.
In April, thousands of film stars, writers and directors, including Jane Fonda, Mark Ruffalo, Denis Villeneuve and J.J. Abrams, signed a letter opposing the merger, warning of fewer jobs and less choice for audiences.
Opposition also surfaced during awards season, with #BlockTheMerger pins and pointed acceptance speeches. Accepting her Emmy last month, Sally Field said: "We can't let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged."
On the other hand, Tom Cruise and James Cameron backed Paramount, as Ellison reaffirmed his commitment to cinema releases. The future of films on the big screen had also been a central concern for critics of Netflix's earlier bid.
Trump and CNN's editorial independence
US President Donald Trump has regularly attacked CNN's reporting and called for the network to be sold during the takeover battle. His administration also welcomed the prospect of Ellison taking control. In March, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said: "The sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better."
Ellison has said editorial independence will be maintained at CNN. Under its settlement with 12 states, the company agreed to establish a "News Editorial Independence Board" covering CNN and CBS. But critics point to turmoil already seen at CBS under Skydance ownership and question how effective the board will be, given Ellison's influence over appointments. The combined company is retaining Mark Thompson as CNN's editor-in-chief.
The scrutiny is heightened by Trump's long-standing ties to the Ellison family, although the president has also continued to criticise CBS coverage under Skydance ownership.
Gulf investment raises concerns over influence
To help fund its Warner buyout, Paramount secured billions of dollars in financial backing from three Gulf countries: Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved the company's request for sizeable indirect ownership by those foreign investors.
Paramount previously disclosed it expected those funds to indirectly own nearly 50% of the combined company's equity, but hold no voting rights. The company asked for clearance for foreign investors to hold up to 100% of indirect equity interests, to account for potential future investments. The FCC granted that request, citing in part that access to more capital would strengthen the broadcast industry and was therefore "in the public interest".
Critics, including the FCC's sole Democratic commissioner, Anna Gomez, have called the move alarming and unprecedented. They argue that such substantial investment opens the door to behind-the-scenes influence.
Settlements clear the final legal hurdles
Paramount cleared antitrust hurdles for its Warner acquisition from regulators worldwide over the summer, including the Trump administration's Justice Department.
But in July, Democratic attorneys general from 12 states, led by California's Rob Bonta, sued to block the merger, alleging the combined company would "extinguish competition" and lead to fewer choices for consumers, particularly cinemagoers and cable customers across the US.
The Writers Guild of America followed suit. Paramount initially agreed to delay completion until next year while the challenges moved towards an antitrust trial.
Settlement agreements emerged in September. The states' terms, eventually approved by a judge, include pledges from the company to increase film production in the US over the next five years, invest in workforce training and career development, and establish an editorial independence board for CNN and CBS.

sources.headline: Paramount completes $81bn takeover of Warner Bros Discovery
Paramount wraps up Warner Bros mega merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
sources.text: Paramount Skydance on Oct 6 completed its blockbuster US$110 billion (S$140.5 billion) takeover of Warner Bros Discovery, creating a Hollywood heavyweight called Skydance and handing chief executive David Ellison control of one of the world’s largest entertainment companies.The deal brings together the studios behind Mission: Impossible, Harry Potter and DC Studios, alongside major television and streaming networks such as CBS, CNN, Paramount+ and HBO Max – forming an expansive entertainment company spanning film, TV and news.Shares of the combined company moved to the New York Stock Exchange from Nasdaq on Oct 6 to trade under the ticker “SKYD”.Settlements with a coalition of US states and a Hollywood writers union removed the main legal barriers to the merger, one of the largest in media history. It comes as Hollywood faces declining cable-TV subscriptions, high cost of competing for streaming audiences and persistent pressure from unions over jobs and creative workers’ rights.Ellison said last week the Skydance name was chosen to retain the individual identities of Paramount and Warner Bros studios, rather than combining them under a new brand.Analysts, however, said the name reinforces the extent of Ellison’s control, highlighting how some of Hollywood’s most iconic brands now answer to him and how he has a platform to impose his strategy and culture.In just 16 years, Skydance has gone from an independent studio to the centre of one of Hollywood’s biggest power plays. Founded in 2010 by the son of Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, it built its reputation as a financial backer and producer of Paramount’s blockbuster Top Gun: Maverick.After merging with Paramount in 2025, Skydance set its sights on Warner Bros, entering a heated bidding contest with Netflix while drawing interest from other potential suitors, including Comcast.Broader Hollywood betEllison named Mattel’s former chief executive officer Ynon Kreiz as Skydance co-chief executive officer to run day-to-day operations and lead the integration, while Ellison oversees creative direction and overall strategy.The duo faces the task of combining two large companies while delivering US$6 billion in planned cost savings, a big part of which Paramount said would come from “non-labour sources” – by combining streaming technologies and cloud providers of the two companies. However, the scale of the cuts is expected to affect jobs across Hollywood.The combined company is also expected to carry about US$80 billion in debt, putting pressure on Ellison to grow streaming, preserve cash flow from cable networks and improve theatrical film performance.CNN chief Mark Thompson and CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss would continue in their respective leadership roles at Skydance. REUTERS
